events.title: One vanishing point
events.line: Florence: artists work out how lines meet at one vanishing point (about 1415 to 1435).

events.title: Printing press
events.line: Printing presses spread across Europe (from the 1450s).

events.title: Brass by sea
events.line: Portuguese ships trade with the Kingdom of Benin (from the 1480s), bringing brass.

events.title: Light from darkness
events.line: Caravaggio paints with strong light out of deep shadow (1590s).

events.title: Photography
events.line: Photography is announced to the world (1839).

events.title: Paint in a tube
events.line: A squeezable metal paint tube is patented (1841). Painters can carry oil paint outside.

events.title: Railways
events.line: Railways reach Paris and the countryside (1830s to 1840s).

events.title: Prints reach Paris
events.line: Japan opens trade with the West (1854 to 1858). Japanese prints reach Paris.

events.title: Color lithography
events.line: Color printing from stone (lithography) makes big posters cheap (1880s to 1890s).

events.title: Lost-wax casting
events.line: Lost-wax casting: a wax model is covered in clay, melted out, and metal is poured in.

events.title: Nature as shapes
events.line: Cezanne paints nature as shapes and patches (1880s to 1900s).

events.title: Abstraction
events.line: Artists paint pictures with no objects at all (1910s).

threads.line: The new perspective method lets Fra Carnevale build a deep, believable street.
Printed in many copies, Durer's rhino became the picture of a rhinoceros in Europe for about 200 years.
Brass from European trade was melted down and cast into palace plaques.
Two places, one method: both were cast by the lost-wax process.

Gentileschi learned from Caravaggio's light, as did many painters of her time.

Once cameras could record exactly, painters like Monet painted light and feeling instead.
Paint in tubes let Cezanne paint his mountain outdoors, again and again.
Monet paints the new railway station itself.
Prints like this one reached Paris after trade opened.
Flat color and flowing outlines from Japanese prints show up in Paris posters.
Mucha's designs were printed in color from stone in large numbers.

Cezanne's shapes led to Cubism, and Mondrian passed through Cubism on his way to pure grids.
Kandinsky was one of the first to paint with no objects.
Mondrian reduced painting to lines and a few colors.
Courbet's real, everyday subjects opened the door for modern-life painting.
1,500 years apart, both paint buildings to make space look deep.
Two ways to show space: a traveling view in China, one fixed viewpoint in Italy.
Painted pots that tell stories, an ocean and centuries apart.
